summary: Children should learn the benchmark decimal names for 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4 (0.5, 0.25, 0.75) by understanding WHY they hold, not just memorising them. The reliable route is through hundredths: 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25 because a quarter of a hundred squares is 25 of them. Grounding this on a 10×10 grid (and a number line where 1/4 and 0.25 mark the same point) helps counter the digit-copying error (1/4 → '0.14' or '0.4') and the denominator-as-count error (shading 4 squares). These three equivalents are high-utility landmarks across the fraction–decimal–percentage web, so children should be able to both recall them and justify them.
misconceptions: Digit-copying: writing 1/4 as 0.14 or 0.4 (treating numerator/denominator digits as decimal digits).
Denominator-as-count on the grid: shading 4 squares for 1/4 (reading 1/4 as 4/100 = 0.04).
Believing 0.25 > 0.5 because '25 > 5' (whole-number bias across the decimal).
Treating the fraction and its decimal as different, unrelated values.
Recalling the facts with no grounding, so errors cannot be self-checked.

activities.title: Shade a quarter: finding 0.25 on the hundred grid
steps: On a 10×10 grid of 100 squares, split the whole into four equal groups and shade one group to make a quarter.
Count the shaded squares (25) and write the result as 25/100, then as the decimal 0.25.
Repeat for one half (50 squares = 50/100 = 0.5) and three-quarters (75 squares = 75/100 = 0.75), building the three as a connected family.
Mark 1/4 and 0.25 on a number line and check they land on the SAME point; do the same for 1/2 = 0.5 and 3/4 = 0.75.
Work in both directions: given a fraction, find the decimal; given the decimal, shade the grid and name the fraction, justifying each with the grid.
activities.insight: A quarter of 100 is 25 squares, so 1/4 and 0.25 name one and the same value — a fact the child can rebuild for 1/2 and 3/4 rather than recall blindly.

activities.title: Predict, then check: why isn't a quarter 4 squares?
steps: Before shading anything, predict how many of the 100 squares you will shade for 1/4, and say WHY.
Then shade a quarter by splitting into four equal groups and taking one; count the squares.
Reconcile the count (25) with your prediction: if you predicted 4, explain what went wrong.
Read off 25/100 = 0.25 and state whether 1/4 and 0.25 are the same value or different.
activities.insight: Making the prediction explicit surfaces the denominator-as-count error ('4, because of the 4 in 1/4') so the child confronts and corrects it against the actual 25 squares.

activities.title: Which is bigger: 0.25 or 0.5?
steps: Shade a quarter (25 squares) and a half (50 squares) on separate hundred grids and compare the shaded areas.
Decide which decimal is larger, 0.25 or 0.5, and explain the choice using the grids rather than the digit strings.
State why '25 is more than 5' does not make 0.25 bigger, referring to tenths and hundredths place value.
Order 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 and check the order against the grids and the number line.
activities.insight: Comparing decimals means comparing by highest place value (tenths first), not by treating the digits after the point as whole numbers; a quarter is clearly less than a half on the grid.

activities.title: Connect to money and matching
steps: Fill in the hundredths chain for each landmark: 1/4 = __/100 = 0.__, 1/2 = __/100 = 0.__, 3/4 = __/100 = 0.__, justifying the denominator-100 step.
Link each equivalent to money as a familiar anchor: £1 = 100p, so a quarter = 25p = £0.25, a half = 50p = £0.50, three-quarters = 75p = £0.75.
Match fraction cards to decimal cards for the three landmarks (1/4↔0.25, 1/2↔0.5, 3/4↔0.75).

Transfer the hundredths route to a new fraction whose denominator divides 100 exactly (for example 1/5 = 20/100 = 0.2 or 1/10 = 10/100 = 0.1), explaining how many of the 100 squares it covers, just as you did for a quarter.
activities.insight: The three equivalents form a reusable family: the denominator-100 route extends to other fractions whose denominators divide 100 exactly (such as tenths, fifths and twentieths), and familiar contexts like money give extra anchors for recall.

checkQuestion: Write 1/4 as a decimal. Then use this 10×10 grid to explain WHY it equals that decimal.
checkAnswer: 1/4 = 0.25. On the grid, a quarter of the 100 squares is 25 squares, so 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25.
